draft.title: Language that gives power
card: Speakers choose words to show authority or to bring listeners in. Four common choices are titles, technical terms, commands and the inclusive we.
Titles and technical terms
A title such as Dr or Captain signals a speaker's role. Specialist words, such as those a pilot or a doctor uses, signal knowledge and can make the speaker sound expert.
Commands
A command, such as "Stand behind the line", tells people what to do. It puts the speaker in charge.
Inclusive we
Words such as we, us and our place the speaker and listeners in the same group. They can build a sense of shared purpose and belonging.
draft.remember: Power language can show who is in charge, or who belongs to the group.

a.q: A coach tells her team, "We can win together." What does the word we mainly do?
opts: Makes the players feel part of one group
Shows the coach's expert technical knowledge
Gives the players a direct order to obey
Shows the coach's official job title
a.why: We places the coach and players in the same group, so it builds belonging. It is not a command, because it gives no instruction, and it is not a technical term.

b.q: At a school assembly, Ms Tran says, "As your principal, I expect hats outside. Hats on, please." Which word choices give her authority?
opts: Her title and the command "Hats on"
The inclusive we and a technical term
A technical term and her friendly tone
Her title and an inclusive our
b.why: Principal is a title that signals her role, and "Hats on" is a command that tells students what to do. The passage has no inclusive we and no specialist words, so the other options name features that are not there.
b.clue: Look for a role word and an instruction.

a.best: Makes the players feel part of one group

b.best: Her title and the command "Hats on"
